Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph
papers.research_question: Does the computational graph of Chain-of-Thought reasoning steps contain structural fingerprints that distinguish correct from incorrect steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a white-box method that uses structural fingerprints from attribution graphs to verify and correct Chain-of-Thought reasoning errors.
papers.conclusion: By analyzing the computational process of LLMs, CRV enables a deeper, causal understanding of reasoning failures, moving beyond simple error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Structural signatures of error in attribution graphs are highly predictive of reasoning correctness.
These signatures are domain-specific, with distinct computational patterns for different reasoning tasks.
The signatures are causal; targeted interventions on transcoder features can correct faulty reasoning.
CRV outperforms black-box and gray-box baselines in verification accuracy.
Error fingerprints are task-specific but can be combined in a multi-task classifier.
papers.limitation:
Computational intensity of CRV makes it impractical for real-time verification.
Aggregative feature analysis does not fully exploit semantic content of individual transcoder features.
Generalizability of error signatures across different model architectures and scales is unproven.
Fidelity of interpretability tools (transcoders, attribution methods) limits analysis resolution.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated classifiers that operate on the semantics of transcoder features.
Studying generalizability of error signatures across model paradigms and scales.
Improving fidelity of interpretability tools for more precise analysis.
papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods predict reasoning correctness based on outputs (black-box) or activations (gray-box), but offer limited insight into why a computation fails. We introduce a white-box method: Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV). We hypothesize that attribution graphs of correct CoT steps, viewed as execution traces of the model's latent reasoning circuits, possess distinct structural fingerprints from those of incorrect steps. By training a classifier on structural features of these graphs, we show that these traces contain a powerful signal of reasoning errors. Our white-box approach yields novel scientific insights unattainable by other methods. (1) We demonstrate that structural signatures of error are highly predictive, establishing the viability of verifying reasoning directly via its computational graph. (2) We find these signatures to be highly domain-specific, revealing that failures in different reasoning tasks manifest as distinct computational patterns. (3) We provide evidence that these signatures are not merely correlational; by using our analysis to guide targeted interventions on individual transcoder features, we successfully correct the model's faulty reasoning. Our work shows that, by scrutinizing a model's computational process, we can move from simple error detection to a deeper, causal understanding of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Overclocking LLM Reasoning: Monitoring and Controlling Thinking Path Lengths in LLMs
papers.abstract: Recently, techniques such as explicit structured reasoning have demonstrated strong test-time scaling behavior by enforcing a separation between the model's internal "thinking" process and the final response. A key factor influencing answer quality in this setting is the length of the thinking stage. When the reasoning is too short, the model may fail to capture the complexity of the task. Conversely, when it is too long, the model may overthink, leading to unnecessary computation and degraded performance. This paper explores and exploits the underlying mechanisms by which LLMs understand and regulate the length of their reasoning during explicit thought processes. First, we show that LLMs encode their progress through the reasoning process and introduce an interactive progress bar visualization, which is then used to reveal insights on the model's planning dynamics. Second, we manipulate the internal progress encoding during inference to reduce unnecessary steps and generate a more concise and decisive chain of thoughts. Our empirical results demonstrate that this "overclocking" method mitigates overthinking, improves answer accuracy, and reduces inference latency. Our code is publicly available.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
papers.research_question: What makes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance? Specifically, are ground truth bridging objects/language templates important, and if not, what are the key aspects needed for the LLM to reason properly?
papers.core_contribution: The validity of reasoning in Chain-of-Thought demonstrations is not crucial for performance; instead, the relevance of the rationale to the query and the coherence (correct ordering) of the reasoning steps are the key aspects that determine the effectiveness of CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: The study deepens understanding of CoT prompting by showing that valid reasoning in demonstrations is not the primary driver of performance; instead, relevance and coherence are critical. This suggests LLMs' reasoning abilities largely come from pretraining, and CoT demonstrations mainly regularize the output format.
papers.key_findings:
Providing demonstrations with completely invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance of standard CoT prompting, indicating that logical validity in the examples is not essential.
Relevance (the rationale being based on the query) and coherence (the correct ordering of steps) are identified as the two key aspects for effective CoT prompting.
Relevance is more important than coherence for bridging objects (e.g., numbers, entities), while coherence of language templates is particularly important.
When both relevance and coherence are removed, performance drops significantly, sometimes below standard prompting without rationales.
The findings suggest LLMs may not be learning to reason from the demonstrations but rather using pretrained abilities, with CoT mainly specifying an output format that regularizes generation to be step-by-step, in order, and relevant.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to two types of reasoning tasks (arithmetic reasoning and multi-hop question answering); other tasks like symbolic reasoning were not studied due to their highly template-based nature.
The construction of invalid reasoning demonstrations was done manually, lacking a systematic treatment; automatically synthesizing such rationales is challenging.
Intrinsic evaluation relies on the correctness of bridging objects, which may not be a comprehensive metric and requires costly annotation.
future_direction: Extending the ablation designs to other types of reasoning tasks, such as symbolic reasoning tasks where steps have little variation.
Developing a more systematic treatment of the 'invalid reasoning' setting, e.g., by categorizing informal logical fallacies.
Improving intrinsic evaluation methods to be more comprehensive and reference-free.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can dramatically improve the multi-step reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). CoT explicitly encourages the LLM to generate intermediate rationales for solving a problem, by providing a series of reasoning steps in the demonstrations. Despite its success, there is still little understanding of what makes CoT prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance. In this paper, we show that CoT reasoning is possible even with invalid demonstrations - prompting with invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance obtained using CoT under various metrics, while still generating coherent lines of reasoning during inference. Further experiments show that other aspects of the rationales, such as being relevant to the query and correctly ordering the reasoning steps, are much more important for effective CoT reasoning. Overall, these findings both deepen our understanding of CoT prompting, and open up new questions regarding LLMs' capability to learn to reason in context.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Identifying and Transferring Reasoning-Critical Neurons: Improving LLM Inference Reliability via Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can activation-level interventions improve LLM reasoning reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaRAS, a test-time activation steering framework that identifies Reasoning-Critical Neurons (RCNs) via mean activation differences and polarity filtering to improve LLM reasoning reliability without additional training.
papers.conclusion: AdaRAS, an inference-time activation steering framework, improves reasoning reliability by identifying and steering Reasoning-Critical Neurons, demonstrating consistent gains across benchmarks and strong transferability.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of MLP neurons exhibits strong predictive correlations with reasoning correctness.
AdaRAS consistently improves reasoning accuracy across 10 mathematics and coding benchmarks, with gains over 13% on some datasets.
The identified Reasoning-Critical Neurons (RCNs) show strong transferability across datasets and tasks.
AdaRAS scales effectively to larger models and outperforms post-training baselines without additional training or sampling cost.
The method stabilizes latent reasoning trajectories without altering semantic modeling, as shown by trajectory-level feature analysis.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focuses on the Qwen3 series models and STEM benchmarks; generalizability to other architectures and complex reasoning settings (e.g., spatial or multi-hop reasoning) needs further evaluation.
Relies on constructing contrastive data pairs, which may limit applicability to models at capability extremes where obtaining paired correct/incorrect reasoning trajectories is non-trivial.
Identifies RCNs using neuron-level activations with the mean difference metric; other advanced techniques (e.g., sparse autoencoders) could provide further mechanistic insights.
future_direction: Extending evaluation to a broader range of model architectures and complex reasoning settings.
Exploring alternative data construction strategies that relax the requirement for contrastive pairs.
Incorporating other advanced techniques, such as sparse autoencoders or vocabulary projection analyses, to further elucidate the mechanistic underpinnings of RCNs.
papers.abstract: Despite the strong reasoning capabilities of recent large language models (LLMs), achieving reliable performance on challenging tasks often requires post-training or computationally expensive sampling strategies, limiting their practical efficiency. In this work, we first show that a small subset of neurons in LLMs exhibits strong predictive correlations with reasoning correctness. Based on this observation, we propose AdaRAS (Adaptive Reasoning Activation Steering), a lightweight test-time framework that improves reasoning reliability by selectively intervening on neuron activations. AdaRAS identifies Reasoning-Critical Neurons (RCNs) via a polarity-aware mean-difference criterion and adaptively steers their activations during inference, enhancing incorrect reasoning traces while avoiding degradation on already-correct cases. Experiments on 10 mathematics and coding benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, including over 13% gains on AIME-24 and AIME-25. Moreover, AdaRAS exhibits strong transferability across datasets and scalability to stronger models, outperforming post-training methods without additional training or sampling cost.

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Language Models with Rationality
papers.research_question: How can we make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit and resolve inconsistencies so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent belief system?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REFLEX, a new system architecture that adds a rational layer on top of an LLM to construct explicit belief graphs and resolve inconsistencies, improving belief consistency without harming answer accuracy.
papers.conclusion: REFLEX is an important step towards improving confidence in system behavior and towards trustable deployment of LLMs in practical applications by providing interpretable reasoning and repairing latent inconsistencies.
papers.key_findings:
REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy.
The rational layer provides faithful explanations by supporting answers with interpretable chains of reasoning from a consistent belief system.
The constraint reasoner can correct initially wrong answers, correct erroneous latent model beliefs, and identify and reject bad rules.
All three types of rules (p → h, XOR, MC) contribute to the system's consistency improvements.
Failure modes include missing rules, incorrect beliefs, incorrect rules, ambiguous statements, and multiple valid answers.
papers.limitation:
The reasoning component can make mistakes, resulting in the overall system rejecting true statements or accepting false ones.
The method is evaluated only on a T5-11B based LLM; effectiveness with newer and larger LLMs like ChatGPT and LLaMA remains to be evaluated.
No formal user study has been conducted to measure the value of belief graphs for providing explanations and gaining user trust.
future_direction: Incorporating the question's context in the belief statements to make semantics more precise and avoid ambiguity.
Using the belief graph to identify uncertain reasoning pieces and guide a human-in-the-loop mechanism for correction or validation.
Maintaining a persistent belief graph over multiple questions to make the system more consistent across questions in a dialog setting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are proficient at question-answering (QA), it is not always clear how (or even if) an answer follows from their latent "beliefs". This lack of interpretability is a growing impediment to widespread use of LLMs. To address this, our goals are to make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit, and to resolve inconsistencies that may exist, so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent network of beliefs. Our approach, which we call REFLEX, is to add a rational, self-reflecting layer on top of the LLM. First, given a question, we construct a belief graph using a backward-chaining process to materialize relevant model beliefs (including beliefs about answer candidates) and their inferential relationships. Second, we identify and minimize contradictions in that graph using a formal constraint reasoner. We find that REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy, resulting in answers supported by faithful chains of reasoning drawn from a more consistent belief system. This suggests a new style of system architecture in which an LLM extended with a rational layer can provide an interpretable window into system beliefs, add a systematic reasoning capability, and repair latent inconsistencies present in the LLM.

papers.title: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the multi-step logical reasoning capabilities of large language models while producing interpretable, causal reasoning traces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Selection-Inference (SI) framework, which decomposes logical reasoning into iterative selection and inference steps using frozen LLMs, significantly improving performance on multi-step reasoning tasks and producing causal, interpretable reasoning traces.
papers.conclusion: The Selection-Inference framework effectively improves the logical reasoning capabilities of LLMs by breaking down problems into iterative selection and inference steps, yielding both performance gains and interpretable, causal reasoning traces.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla LLMs perform well on single-step inference but struggle with multi-step logical reasoning.
The SI framework with a 7B LLM almost triples the performance of the same model used naively and outperforms a 40x larger 280B LLM baseline on a suite of logical reasoning tasks.
The SI framework produces causal, natural language reasoning traces that justify the final answer, aiding interpretability and trust.
The modular design of SI allows for error recovery and human inspection of intermediate reasoning steps.
Fine-tuning the Selection and Inference modules on single reasoning steps further improves performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.limitation:
The main point of failure tends to be the Selection module, which is difficult to quantify without labeled data for intermediate steps.
The approach assumes a database of facts or rules is given, which may not be available in practical settings requiring knowledge retrieval.
The model uses a fixed compute budget (number of steps) and lacks a mechanism for deciding when to halt the reasoning process or filtering reasoning traces.
future_direction: Combine the SI model with knowledge retrieval methods to relax the assumption of given context.
Address the halting problem and develop mechanisms to filter reasoning traces and select the best answer.
Explore fine-tuning the modules for specific tasks to improve performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be capable of impressive few-shot generalisation to new tasks. However, they still tend to perform poorly on multi-step logical reasoning problems. Here we carry out a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on 50 tasks that probe different aspects of logical reasoning. We show that language models tend to perform fairly well at single step inference or entailment tasks, but struggle to chain together multiple reasoning steps to solve more complex problems. In light of this, we propose a Selection-Inference (SI) framework that exploits pre-trained LLMs as general processing modules, and alternates between selection and inference to generate a series of interpretable, casual reasoning steps leading to the final answer. We show that a 7B parameter LLM used within the SI framework in a 5-shot generalisation setting, with no fine-tuning, yields a performance improvement of over 100% compared to an equivalent vanilla baseline on a suite of 10 logical reasoning tasks. The same model in the same setting even outperforms a significantly larger 280B parameter baseline on the same suite of tasks. Moreover, answers produced by the SI framework are accompanied by a causal natural-language-based reasoning trace, which has important implications for the safety and trustworthiness of the system.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Soundness-Aware Level: A Microscopic Signature that Predicts LLM Reasoning Potential
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can elicit strong reasoning in large language models (LLMs), while their performance after RLVR varies dramatically across different base models. This raises a fundamental question: what microscopic property of pre-trained models leads to this variation? To investigate, we formalize reasoning as chains of Horn clauses ("if-then" rules) built from features extracted from the LLM's latent space via cross-layer sparse autoencoders (SAEs). We estimate the transition probabilities between its features, and further categorize each rule by its semantic soundness level (e.g., strict, plausible, noisy) with an LLM. Our key discovery is that high-potential models are inherently soundness-aware: their internal probability distributions systematically shift across rules' soundness levels, becoming highly distinct for "strict" versus "noisy" rules. In contrast, weaker models are soundness-agnostic, collapsing to one distribution regardless of soundness levels. To quantify this, we introduce the Soundness-Aware Level (SAL), a microscopic metric using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence to measure the separation between these distributions. We show that SAL's predictions of post-RLVR reasoning performance follow a precise empirical law (R^2=0.87) across diverse model families (Qwen, Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek) and scales (0.5B-14B). This reveals that a model's reasoning potential is tied to its intrinsic, pre-trained ability to distinguish sound knowledge from unsound ones. These findings underscore the critical role of model pre-training in shaping reasoning and offer a practical metric grounded in the model's internal mechanisms for selecting/designing stronger base models.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Weight-of-Thought Reasoning: Exploring Neural Network Weights for Enhanced LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can neural network weights be examined before inference to identify and enhance reasoning pathways in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Weight-of-Thought reasoning, a novel approach that analyzes neural network weights prior to inference to identify and structure latent reasoning pathways, leading to improved performance and interpretability on complex reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Weight-of-Thought reasoning represents a significant step toward more structured, efficient, and interpretable reasoning in neural networks by leveraging the weight space, offering a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
WoT reasoning outperforms traditional methods like Chain-of-Thought on diverse reasoning tasks, especially complex multi-step problems.
The WoT model achieves superior performance with only ~2M parameters, demonstrating high parameter efficiency compared to large LLM baselines (~175B parameters).
Ablation studies show that weight-directed guidance, graph-based message passing, node specialization, and iterative refinement are all critical components contributing to WoT's performance.
Internal analysis reveals node specialization and dynamic, task-adaptive information flow within the reasoning graph.
WoT's graph structure enables parallel processing and adaptive information routing, moving beyond sequential reasoning chains.
papers.limitation:
Generalization capability across all types of reasoning problems requires further investigation.
The all-to-all message passing mechanism scales quadratically with the number of reasoning nodes, posing potential scaling challenges.
Performance is contingent on the quality and diversity of the training data.
Integrating WoT principles directly within the architecture of extremely large, pre-existing language models presents non-trivial technical hurdles.
Evaluation primarily relies on accuracy and MSE metrics, which may not fully encompass all facets of reasoning quality.
future_direction: Investigating generalization across broader reasoning problem types.
Addressing the quadratic scaling challenge of the message passing mechanism.
Developing integration techniques for large pre-existing language models and broader evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities when prompted with strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT).However, these approaches focus on token-level output without considering internal weight dynamics.We introduce Weight-of-Thought (WoT) reasoning, a novel approach that examines neural network weights before inference to identify reasoning pathways.Unlike existing methods, WoT explores the weight space through graph-based message passing, multi-step reasoning processes, and attention mechanisms.Our implementation creates an interconnected graph of reasoning nodes.Experiments on diverse reasoning tasks (syllogistic, mathematical, algebraic, combinatorial, and geometric) demonstrate that WoT achieves superior performance compared to traditional methods, particularly for complex problems.This approach leads to both improved performance and greater interpretability of the reasoning process, offering a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct.
